title: Geometry-Aware Similarity Metrics for Neural Representations on Riemannian and Statistical Manifolds
claim: Similarity measured on intrinsic geometry can diverge from extrinsic similarity, so intrinsic comparison reveals computational differences that extrinsic metrics miss.
layout: 3 columns: surface pairs left and right flank two bar charts, arrows converge
description: Three-part symmetric figure. At left, two 3D-rendered blue gridded surfaces are stacked. The top one is a flat Euclidean plane and the bottom one is a rolled-up Swiss roll. Each carries a small black triangle that marks the preserved local geometry. At right, two more blue gridded surfaces are stacked. The top one is a flat plane and the bottom one is a warped plane with distorted grid lines, which stands for a non-Euclidean plane. Grey arrows from each pair point inward at a bar chart in the centre. The y-axis is labelled Similarity and runs from 0.0 to 1.0. Each chart has a dark grey bar for extrinsic similarity and an orange bar for intrinsic similarity. Left pair: low extrinsic, high intrinsic. Right pair: high extrinsic, low intrinsic. A legend below reads Extrinsic in dark slate and Intrinsic in orange. Small axis glyphs sit beside each surface. The eye goes first to the central bars, then outward to the surfaces.
caption: Intrinsic vs. extrinsic similarity. \rd{The Euclidean plane and Swiss roll can have high intrinsic similarity (MSA) yet low extrinsic similarity (Procrustes), and conversely for a Euclidean vs. non-Euclidean plane. We argue that the intrinsic geometry of representations is more insightful for comparing computations.}
abstract: Similarity measures such as centred kernel alignment (CKA) or representational similarity analysis (RSA) are widely used to compare the representational geometries employed by different neural networks to solve the same task. Yet, because existing methods compare the extrinsic geometry of representations in state space, rather than their intrinsic geometry, they may fail to capture subtle yet crucial distinctions between fundamentally different computations. Here, we introduce metric similarity analysis (MSA), a novel method which leverages tools from Riemannian geometry to compare the intrinsic geometry of neural representations under the manifold hypothesis. We show that MSA can be used to (i) disentangle neural computations of deep networks in rich vs. lazy learning regimes, (ii) compare the dynamics of recurrent neural networks and state-space models, and (iii) investigate the statistical manifolds of diffusion models. Overall, we introduce a mathematically grounded and broadly applicable framework to understand the mechanisms behind neural computations by contrasting their intrinsic geometries.
